5.2 Row-standardised Weights Matrix
nb2listw() of spdep turns the neighbour list into weights. style = "W" divides each county’s weights by its number of neighbours. So the lag of a county is the simple average of its neighbours.

rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
rswm_q

W 88 7744 88 37.86334 365.9147








NoteLearning diary



zero.policy = TRUE lets spdep accept a county with no neighbours instead of stopping with an error. Hunan has no such county, so it changes nothing here. The book always sets it, and it matters for data with islands.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.1 Moran’s I Test
moran.test() of spdep computes Moran’s I. It tests it against the null hypothesis that GDPPC is spread across the counties at random. The default alternative is "greater", so the test only looks for positive autocorrelation.

moran_gdppc <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC,
                          listw = rswm_q,
                          zero.policy = TRUE,
                          na.action = na.omit)
moran_gdppc


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC  
weights: rswm_q    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.7351, p-value = 1.095e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351 


Moran’s I is 0.301 against an expected value of -0.0115 under randomness. The p-value is 1.1e-06, far below 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis. GDPPC in Hunan is positively autocorrelated. Rich counties tend to sit next to rich counties and poor ones next to poor ones.






ImportantCheck that caught something



In Exercise 4 I predicted this number before running any test. The slope of the neighbour average on GDPPC was 0.301. I argued that with row-standardised weights this slope equals Moran’s I. The test gives the same value to three decimals, so I was right. moran.test() adds the p-value.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.2 Computing Monte Carlo Moran’s I
moran.mc() of spdep runs a permutation test instead. It shuffles GDPPC across the 88 counties 999 times and computes Moran’s I for each shuffle. Then it counts how often a shuffle beats the real map. set.seed() makes the result the same on every render.

set.seed(1234)
bperm <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                  listw = rswm_q,
                  nsim = 999,
                  zero.policy = TRUE,
                  na.action = na.omit)
bperm


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.30075, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


The observed I ranks 1000 out of 1000, above all 999 shuffles. This gives a p-value of 0.001, the same conclusion as the analytical test. A random arrangement of these values does not produce this clustering.






NoteLearning diary



The p-value of 0.001 is the lowest possible value here. With 999 shuffles plus the real map there are 1,000 values. The real map can at best rank first, so the smallest p-value is 1/1000. Running 9,999 shuffles would lower this floor but not change the conclusion. The analytical test can go much smaller because it uses a normal approximation instead of counting.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.3 Visualising Monte Carlo Moran’s I
mean(), var() and summary() describe the 999 simulated values. bperm$res also holds the observed I as its last element. This is why the book slices [1:999].

mean(bperm$res[1:999])

[1] -0.01504572

var(bperm$res[1:999])

[1] 0.004371574

summary(bperm$res[1:999])

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
-0.18339 -0.06168 -0.02125 -0.01505  0.02611  0.27593 


The book asks me to redraw the histogram with ggplot2 instead of base graphics. geom_histogram() draws the 999 simulated values. The dashed line marks the expected value under randomness, -1/(n - 1), and the orange line marks the observed I.

The PlotThe Code














mc_moran <- tibble(sim = bperm$res[1:999])

ggplot(mc_moran, aes(x = sim)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1 / (nrow(hunan) - 1),
             linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bperm$statistic,
             colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = bperm$statistic, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("Observed I = ", round(bperm$statistic, 3)),
           hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.5, colour = "#D55E00", size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Moran's I, 999 shuffles against the real map",
       subtitle = "Dashed line, expected I under randomness, -1/87") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))




The shuffles centre on -0.015, close to the expected -1/87, with a standard deviation of about 0.066. The highest of the 999 is 0.276. The observed 0.301 is beyond all of them, which matches the rank of 1000. The simulated distribution is slightly skewed to the right, so the normal approximation behind moran.test() is only approximate.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
7.1 Geary’s C Test
geary.test() of spdep computes Geary’s C. It works the opposite way to Moran’s I. The expected value under randomness is 1. Values below 1 mean neighbours are similar, and values above 1 mean they are different.

geary_gdppc <- geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)
geary_gdppc


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 3.6108, p-value = 0.0001526
alternative hypothesis: Expectation greater than statistic
sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
        0.6907223         1.0000000         0.0073364 


Geary’s C is 0.691, below the expected 1, with a p-value of 0.00015. So Geary’s C also rejects randomness. Like Moran’s I, it shows positive autocorrelation.






NoteLearning diary



The two statistics are built differently, so they can disagree. Moran’s I multiplies each county’s deviation from the mean by its neighbours’ deviations. It is a covariance and responds to the overall trend across the province. Geary’s C squares the difference between each pair of neighbours. It is closer to a local variance and responds more to sharp differences between next-door counties. Here they agree.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
7.2 Computing Monte Carlo Geary’s C
geary.mc() of spdep runs the same permutation idea for Geary’s C.

set.seed(1234)
bperm_c <- geary.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                    listw = rswm_q,
                    nsim = 999)
bperm_c


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Geary C

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.69072, observed rank = 1, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater








CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book stores this result in bperm again, which overwrites the Moran’s I permutations. I call it bperm_c so both stay available for the comparison below.


The observed C ranks 1, lower than every shuffle. For Geary’s C the small end is the extreme end. So a rank of 1 gives the same lowest p-value of 0.001.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
8.1 Compute Moran’s I Correlogram
sp.correlogram() of spdep computes Moran’s I at lags 1 to 6 with row-standardised weights.

MI_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q,
                          hunan$GDPPC,
                          order = 6,
                          method = "I",
                          style = "W")


The PlotThe Code














plot_corr(corr_table(MI_corr), "Moran's I",
          "Moran's I correlogram of GDPPC")




print() shows the numbers behind the plot, with a p-value for each lag.

print(MI_corr)

Spatial correlogram for hunan$GDPPC 
method: Moran's I
         estimate expectation   variance standard deviate Pr(I) two sided    
1 (88)  0.3007500  -0.0114943  0.0043484           4.7351       2.189e-06 ***
2 (88)  0.2060084  -0.0114943  0.0020962           4.7505       2.029e-06 ***
3 (88)  0.0668273  -0.0114943  0.0014602           2.0496        0.040400 *  
4 (88)  0.0299470  -0.0114943  0.0011717           1.2107        0.226015    
5 (88) -0.1530471  -0.0114943  0.0012440          -4.0134       5.984e-05 ***
6 (88) -0.1187070  -0.0114943  0.0016791          -2.6164        0.008886 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Similarity fades with distance and then turns negative. Lags 1 to 3 are positive and significant, at 0.30, 0.21 and 0.07. So a county is like its neighbours and its neighbours’ neighbours. Lag 4 looks random. Lags 5 and 6 are negative and significant, so counties five steps apart tend to be unlike each other. This fits one rich core with a poorer area around it. Five steps from the Changsha block reaches the far west and south, the other end of the income scale.
The p-values in print() are two-sided and not corrected. Six tests at 0.05 is a small multiple testing problem. But lags 1, 2 and 5 are so far below any threshold that the conclusion holds.

This is the same six lags with Geary’s C.

print(GC_corr)

Spatial correlogram for hunan$GDPPC 
method: Geary's C
        estimate expectation  variance standard deviate Pr(I) two sided    
1 (88) 0.6907223   1.0000000 0.0073364          -3.6108       0.0003052 ***
2 (88) 0.7630197   1.0000000 0.0049126          -3.3811       0.0007220 ***
3 (88) 0.9397299   1.0000000 0.0049005          -0.8610       0.3892612    
4 (88) 1.0098462   1.0000000 0.0039631           0.1564       0.8757128    
5 (88) 1.2008204   1.0000000 0.0035568           3.3673       0.0007592 ***
6 (88) 1.0773386   1.0000000 0.0058042           1.0151       0.3100407    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Geary’s C gives the same result in reverse. It is below 1 at lags 1 and 2, near 1 at lags 3 and 4, and above 1 at lag 5. It is less certain at the ends. Lags 3 and 6 are significant for Moran’s I but not for Geary’s C. This fits the learning diary note above. Geary’s C uses squared differences between the counties being compared. So it responds more to how alike those pairs are, and less to the broad north east against south west trend that Moran’s I picks up.

9.1 Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights with sfdep
st_contiguity() of sfdep builds the Queen neighbour list and st_weights() row-standardises it. Both go into the sf data frame as list columns, and .before = 1 puts them at the front.

  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),

lisa <- hunan_q %>%
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 999),

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
9.3 Mapping Local Moran’s I Values
tm_polygons() maps ii with pretty breaks. midpoint = 0 centres the diverging palette on zero. Blue means a county similar to its neighbours, and red means one that differs from them.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 5,
                                              midpoint = 0,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              col = "grey60") +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I of GDPPC, Queen contiguity",
           size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")




Most of the province is just above zero, in pale blue. These counties are a little like their neighbours and add a little to the global 0.30. The strong contributions all come from a block of dark blue counties around Changsha, with local values of 3 to 5. The red counties have negative values and differ from their neighbours. They sit around the edge of that block and down the south east.

text:
9.5 Mapping Both Local Moran’s I Values and p-values
tmap_arrange() puts the two maps side by side, so I can read a county’s value and its significance together.

The PlotThe Code














ii_map <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 5,
                                              midpoint = 0,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              col = "grey60") +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I", size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")

p_ii_map <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
                labels = c("below 0.001", "0.001 to 0.01", "0.01 to 0.05",
                           "0.05 to 0.1", "above 0.1"),
                values = "-brewer.reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "p-value",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              col = "grey60") +
  tm_title("p-values", size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")

tmap_arrange(ii_map, p_ii_map, ncol = 2)




The dark blue block and the dark red p-values line up almost exactly. So the strongest local values are also the most significant. The south west is different. Its local values are small, but two counties there are significant. A modest positive value among consistently poor neighbours is still unlikely by chance. The value map alone would miss them.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
10.1 Plotting the Moran Scatterplot
st_lag() of sfdep computes the spatial lag, the average GDPPC of each county’s neighbours.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(lag_GDPPC = st_lag(GDPPC, nb, wt),
         .before = 1)







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book follows st_lag() with unnest(lag_GDPPC). st_lag() already returns a plain numeric vector with one value per county. There is nothing to unnest, so I leave that step out.


The Moran scatterplot puts each county’s GDPPC on the x axis and its lag on the y axis. Dashed lines split it into four quadrants. The colour is the quadrant sfdep assigned in the mean column. geom_text_repel() of ggrepel names the counties in the two outlier quadrants.

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(lisa, aes(x = GDPPC, y = lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(lisa$GDPPC), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(lisa$GDPPC), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = mean), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(lisa, mean %in% c("High-Low", "Low-High"),
                                GDPPC > 40000 | lag_GDPPC > 40000),
                  aes(label = NAME_3), size = 3.5, seed = 42,
                  box.padding = 0.5, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High-High" = "#D55E00", "Low-Low" = "#0072B2",
                                 "Low-High" = "#56B4E9", "High-Low" = "#CC79A7")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDPPC (RMB)", y = "Spatial lag of GDPPC (RMB)", colour = "Quadrant",
       title = "Moran scatterplot with LISA quadrants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book’s note says the upper right quadrant holds counties with high GDPPC “surrounded by average-level neighbouring areas”. This does not match what the quadrant means. Upper right is above the mean on both axes. So it is a High-High county, with high GDPPC and neighbours that are also high on average. Counties with average neighbours would sit near the horizontal dashed line, not in a corner.


The book draws the horizontal line at the mean of the lag. I draw both lines at the mean of GDPPC, because that is where the quadrant labels are cut. spdep, which sfdep calls underneath, centres GDPPC at its mean and then lags the centred values.   mutate(label_high = str_detect(mean, "-High$")) %>%
  summarise(`Line at mean of GDPPC` = sum((lag_GDPPC > mean(GDPPC)) == label_high),

The book standardises the lag separately with scale(lag_GDPPC), which divides it by its own standard deviation. Anselin’s standardised Moran scatterplot lags the z-scores instead. Both axes are divided by the same standard deviation. The slope stays at Moran’s I, and zero on both axes is exactly the quadrant boundary. The fitted slope here is 0.301, the same as moran.test(). I also wrap scale() in as.numeric(), because it returns a one-column matrix rather than a vector.

text:
11.1 Deriving Distance Weight Matrix
Gi* is usually run with distance based weights. The book builds two kinds.

Computing fixed distance weightsComputing adaptive distance weights


critical_threshold() of sfdep finds the smallest distance at which every county has at least one neighbour.

ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(hunan))
ct

[1] 62954.89


st_dist_band() makes every county within that distance a neighbour. include_self() adds each county to its own neighbour list, and st_weights() row-standardises.

hunan_fdw <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = ct)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)



st_knn() of sfdep takes each county’s six nearest neighbours instead of a fixed radius.

hunan_adw <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(st_geometry(geometry), k = 6)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)










NoteLearning diary



include_self() is what puts the star in Gi. The plain Gi statistic compares a county’s neighbours with the rest of the province and leaves the county out. Gi counts the county as part of its own neighbourhood. So one very rich county can make its own area a hot spot. This matters for Changsha, which is far richer than anything around it.
My cut-off is 63 km, against the book’s 60.8 km in zone 50. It also does not match Exercise 4, where the same UTM 49N projection with st_centroid() gave 58.3 km. The chunk below computes the cut-off from centroids and from st_point_on_surface() to see which point sfdep uses.



nn_cutoff <- function(pts) {
  xy <- st_coordinates(pts)
  max(unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 1)), xy)))
}

round(c(centroid = nn_cutoff(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan))),
        point_on_surface = nn_cutoff(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(hunan))),
        sfdep = ct))

        centroid point_on_surface            sfdep 
           58337            62955            62955 


The sfdep cut-off matches the point on surface version exactly. The centroid version gives the 58.3 km from Exercise 4. So sfdep measures from st_point_on_surface(), a point that always falls inside each polygon, not from the centroid. The difference between the two exercises came from the point used for each county, not from the projection.

text:
12.1 Does Moran’s I Survive a Different Weights Matrix
Exercise 4 ended with the point that the weights matrix is a choice I make. Every test above used Queen contiguity. Below I rerun moran.test() with four neighbour rules from that exercise, all row-standardised, to see whether the answer depends on the choice. The distance rules use the county centroids in UTM 49N and the cut-off ct from the hot spot section.

coords <- st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan))

w_list <- list(
  "Queen contiguity"     = nb2listw(poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE), style = "W"),
  "Rook contiguity"      = nb2listw(poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE), style = "W"),
  "Fixed distance"       = nb2listw(dnearneigh(coords, 0, ct),
                                    style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
  "Six nearest neighbours" = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6)),
                                      style = "W")
)

moran_by_w <- imap_dfr(w_list, function(lw, rule) {
  t <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  tibble(`Neighbour rule` = rule,
         `Average neighbours` = round(mean(card(lw$neighbours)), 1),
         `Moran's I` = round(t$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]], 3),
         `Standard deviate` = round(t$statistic[[1]], 2),
         `p-value` = format.pval(t$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 1e-8))
})

text:
12.2 Analytical Against Permutation p-values
The LISA map above follows the book and uses p_ii, the analytical p-value. It treats z_ii as a standard normal, which assumes GDPPC is roughly normal. It is not. Changsha is at 88,656 RMB and the median county is near 20,000, so there is a long right tail. The permutation p-value p_ii_sim does not need this assumption. Anselin (1995) recommends the permutation approach for this reason.
There is a second problem. The map runs 88 tests at 0.05 at once, so about four counties would be significant even if GDPPC were random. p.adjust() with the false discovery rate method is one standard correction for this.
summarise() counts how many counties fall below 0.05 under each version.

lisa %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(`Analytical, p_ii` = sum(p_ii < signif),
            `Permutation, p_ii_sim` = sum(p_ii_sim < signif),
            `Folded permutation, p_folded_sim` = sum(p_folded_sim < signif),
            `Permutation after FDR correction` =
              sum(p.adjust(p_ii_sim, method = "fdr") < signif)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = "p-value used",
               values_to = "Counties below 0.05") %>%
  kable()




p-value used
Counties below 0.05




Analytical, p_ii
13


Permutation, p_ii_sim
16


Folded permutation, p_folded_sim
23


Permutation after FDR correction
0





The two cluster maps below use the same colours. The book’s version is on the left and the permutation version on the right.

The PlotThe Code














lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(LISA_sim = if_else(p_ii_sim < signif,
                            as.character(mean), "Insignificant"),
         LISA_sim = factor(LISA_sim, levels = levels(LISA_cluster)))

cluster_map <- function(var, title) {
  tm_shape(lisa) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                  values = c("grey90",   # Insignificant
                           "#0072B2",  # Low-Low
                           "#56B4E9",  # Low-High
                           "#CC79A7",  # High-Low
                           "#D55E00"   # High-High
                           )),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA cluster",
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey60") +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(cluster_map("LISA_cluster", "Analytical p-values"),
             cluster_map("LISA_sim", "Permutation p-values"),
             ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



The choice of p-value changes the map. The analytical p-value finds 13 significant counties, the permutation p-value finds 16, and the folded permutation p-value finds 23. The folded version is in effect one-sided and roughly halves every p-value. The permutation map drops the Low-High county west of Changsha. It adds a larger Low-Low area in the south west and a new one in the north west. Only the High-High core around Changsha stays in every version.
After the false discovery rate correction, none of the 88 counties is significant. With 999 permutations no p-value can go below about 0.001. The correction needs many values that small before it lets any through. It also assumes the tests are independent, but neighbouring counties share neighbours. So the LISA map shows where to look, not a list of proven clusters. Anselin says the same in the 1995 paper. He treats the local p-values as approximate and suggests a Bonferroni style bound as the conservative option.

12.3 Fixed Against Adaptive Hot Spots
The book builds hunan_adw, the six nearest neighbour weights, but never uses it. I run the same Gi* test on those weights to see whether the hot and cold spots depend on the neighbour rule.

  mutate(gistar = local_gstar_perm(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 999),
         .before = 1) %>%

count(st_drop_geometry(HCSA_adw), HCSA_cluster)

  HCSA_cluster      n
  <fct>         <int>
1 Insignificant    69
2 Hot spot         11
3 Cold spot         8



The PlotThe Code














hcsa_map <- function(df, title) {
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "HCSA_cluster",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                  values = c("grey90",   # Insignificant
                           "#D55E00",  # Hot spot
                           "#0072B2"   # Cold spot
                           )),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "HCSA cluster",
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey60") +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(hcsa_map(HCSA_fdw, paste0("Fixed distance, ", round(ct / 1000, 1), " km")),
             hcsa_map(HCSA_adw, "Six nearest neighbours"),
             ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



The hot and cold spots move with the neighbour rule. With six nearest neighbours there are 11 hot spots and 8 cold spots, against 7 and 7 on the fixed band. The hot core grows east to include Pingjiang and west to include Taojiang. The south western cold belt gets longer, and the north western cold group shrinks to a single county.
The rules disagree most in the north west. Its counties are large and far apart. So the fixed band gives them few neighbours, and a few poor counties dominate their own neighbourhood. Six nearest neighbours always reach six counties, often further away, which dilutes them. The core around Changsha and the south western belt appear under both rules, so I trust those most. The north western cold spot depends on the rule.

kbb_sf <- st_read("data/rawdata/gadm/gadm41_IDN_2.json") %>%

3.2 Importing and Preparing Forest Fire Data
FIRMS publishes MODIS detections as one file per country per year. The all-countries bundle arrived cut off at 43 of 82 MB, with Indonesia in the missing part, so I downloaded the Indonesia file directly.

Importing the Indonesia fileChecking the type column


read_csv() of readr (part of tidyverse) reads the file, and nrow() counts the rows.

fire_all <- read_csv("data/rawdata/modis/modis_2023_Indonesia.csv")
nrow(fire_all)

[1] 52156




This is every detection in Indonesia for 2023. Before clipping to the study area, I check one column the book never mentions. table() counts the rows of each type.

table(fire_all$type)


    0     1     2     3 
47883  1495  2755    23 











CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book keeps every row and calls them all forest fires. The type column shows that some are not.
Type 0 is a presumed vegetation fire. Type 1 is an active volcano. Type 2 is another static land source, such as gas flares or industrial heat. Type 3 is offshore. Indonesia has many volcanoes and flares, and 4,250 detections are one or the other (1,495 volcano, 2,755 static source), and another 23 are offshore.
A volcano that shows up every day at the same spot would look like strong spatio-temporal clustering. But it is not a fire. I keep type 0 only.



Filtering and clippingDeriving the time fields


filter() keeps type 0, st_as_sf() turns the longitude and latitude into points, st_transform() projects them to the same UTM zone as the boundary, and st_filter() of sf keeps only the points inside Bangka Belitung.

fire_sf <- fire_all %>%
  filter(type == 0) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748) %>%
  st_filter(st_as_sf(kbb_sf))

nrow(fire_sf)

[1] 897








NoteLearning diary



The book’s csv was already cut to Bangka Belitung, so it has no clipping step. Mine covers all of Indonesia, so st_filter() keeps only the points that intersect the boundary polygon.
My count differs from the book’s 741, as expected. The boundary source is different, and the type filter removed one static-source row that the book would have kept.




as.ppp() only accepts numbers or text as marks, so the date has to become a number. yday() and month() of lubridate (part of tidyverse) give three versions for three uses later on.

fire_sf <- fire_sf %>%
  mutate(acq_date = as.Date(acq_date),
         DayofYear = yday(acq_date),
         Month_num = month(acq_date),
         Month_fac = month(acq_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))

text:
5.3 Plotting the Spatio-Temporal KDE Object
sparr’s plot() method draws one time slice per call. It also adds axis(1), axis(2) and an L-shaped box to every panel. So my first version labelled each small map in projected metres like 9.7e+06, which mean nothing to a reader and got cut off at the edges. The function below draws one slice with spatstat’s plot() for pixel images and adds the window outline, without the axes. It takes the colour range as an argument so panels can share one scale.

plot_slice <- function(kde, t, zlim, main) {
  tt <- as.numeric(names(kde$z))
  slice <- kde$z[[which.min(abs(tt - t))]]
  plot(slice, main = main, zlim = zlim, box = FALSE,
       ribargs = list(box = TRUE))
  plot(as.polygonal(Window(kde$pp)), add = TRUE)
}







NoteLearning diary



The obvious fix is par(xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n") before the loop. But that would also remove the numbers on the colour ribbon. spatstat draws those with axis() on side 4, and a global yaxt = "n" turns that off too. The source of plot.stden() is a short loop around a plot.im() call, so I copied the two lines I needed.


The panels show July to December. The colour key is the estimated joint density, the share of the year’s detections per square metre per month, so the numbers are tiny (the peak is about 6.4e-10). zlim_month is the range over all twelve monthly surfaces, so the six panels share one colour scale.

The PlotThe Code














zlim_month <- range(sapply(st_kde$z, range))
tims <- c(7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
par(mfcol = c(2, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0), cex.main = 1.8)
for (i in tims) {
  plot_slice(st_kde, i, zlim = zlim_month,
             main = paste(month.name[i], "2023"))
}
mtext("Monthly fire intensity, July to December 2023", outer = TRUE, cex = 2.1, font = 2)
par(mfcol = c(1, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0))




The shared zlim works like sparr’s fix.range = TRUE, which uses the same range for every time slice. Without it each month gets its own scale, and a quiet December looks as busy as a peak September.

7.2 Plotting the Output Spatio-Temporal KDE
These are the same six days from the bootstrap surface, in the same unit as above. But this figure has its own zlim_boot, so I compare patterns between the two figures, not colours.

             main = paste0("Day ", d, " (", format(as.Date("2023-01-01") + d - 1, "%d %b"), ")"))
}
mtext("Daily fire intensity, bootstrap bandwidths", outer = TRUE, cex = 2.1, font = 2)
par(mfcol = c(1, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0))










NoteLearning diary



The default gave h of about 19 km and lambda of about 6 days. The bootstrap gave 45 km and 17 days. So the bootstrap smooths more on both axes, more than twice in space and nearly three times in time.
Both sets of maps show the same pattern. A hotspot starts in west Bangka in early August and moves to the south of the island by late September. Belitung stays quiet the whole time.
The default keeps the hotspot tight and Belitung dark. The bootstrap spreads the same hotspot across half of Bangka and halves its peak (the summaries give a maximum of 1.9e-12 for the default and 1.0e-12 for the bootstrap). It also makes Belitung light up, because a 45 km kernel reaches across the strait.
Which one to use depends on the question. For where fires happen, the default’s sharper space is more useful. For when they happen, the bootstrap’s smoother time is better. The bootstrap minimises one overall error and does not know which question I am asking.
The book got 9 km and 19 days on its 741 points, which is sharper in space than its own default. With the same method on a different sample, the spatial bandwidth moved the other way. So the bandwidth depends on the data in hand.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
8.2 Computing Spatio-Temporal K-Function
STIKhat() of stpp estimates the space-time K function on a default grid of spatial and temporal distances.

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)







WarningIssue I hit



The book’s plotK(kbb_stik) rendered nothing. The chunk ran, but the page had an empty tab where the surface should be.
The function source explains why. plotK() closes the current graphics device and opens a new one for its own layout. Knitr was recording into the device that got closed, so the plot went to a window nobody saw.
My fix was to skip plotK() and draw the surface myself. The object holds Khat, the estimate, and Ktheo, the value expected if space and time were independent. Both are over dist and times. I plot the difference, which the reading below uses, and label the axes properly.


filled.contour() from base graphics draws the difference as a coloured surface, and contour() adds labelled lines on top. STIKhat() returns distances in metres, so I divide u by 1000 to put the x axis in kilometres. The colour key, titled “K excess”, is Khat minus Ktheo. It is in the K function’s own units, square metres times days.

The PlotThe Code














u <- kbb_stik$dist / 1000
v <- kbb_stik$times
k_excess <- kbb_stik$Khat - kbb_stik$Ktheo

par(cex.main = 1.3)
filled.contour(u, v, k_excess,
               color.palette = function(n) hcl.colors(n, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
               xlab = "u, spatial distance (km)",
               ylab = "v, temporal distance (days)",
               main = "Space-time K minus the independence expectation",
               key.title = title(main = "K excess", cex.main = 0.9),
               plot.axes = {
                 axis(1); axis(2)
                 contour(u, v, k_excess, add = TRUE, col = "grey10", lwd = 0.6,
                         labcex = 0.9)
               })

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
8.3 Guide to Interpreting the Plot






NoteLearning diary



This plot took me a while to read.
The plot is a surface over two axes. u is distance in space, which I plotted in kilometres, and v is distance in days. The height is how many more fires lie within u kilometres and v days of a typical fire than expected if space and time were independent. This is the Khat minus Ktheo I drew above.
If the surface rises steeply near the origin, at small u and small v, fires happen close to other fires and soon after them. That is space-time clustering. A flat surface means no such interaction.
The name says inhomogeneous, but the call above is not. STIKhat() only corrects for varying intensity if you pass it a lambda, the intensity at every point. The book does not pass one and neither did I. So it uses a constant, the point count divided by the space-time volume, and is really a homogeneous K.
The surface shows this. The excess is positive everywhere and keeps rising with both u and v, out to 45 km and 80 days. Clustering that keeps growing with scale comes from the dry season and the fire belt of Bangka. The KDE already found both. It does not show fires near fires setting off more fires.
A proper inhomogeneous version would pass the spatio-temporal KDE in as lambda. I want to use that version for the take-home.

  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748) %>%
  st_filter(st_as_sf(kbb_sf))

tibble(

  detections = c(nrow(fire_all_kbb), nrow(fire_sf)),

# A tibble: 2 × 3

1 all types          898       0
2 type 0 only        897       1

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   type detections

9.2 Does Detection Confidence Change the Answer
MODIS gives every detection a confidence score from 0 to 100. The book ignores it. quantile() shows how the scores are spread.

quantile(fire_sf$confidence, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1))

  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
   0   55   67   76  100 


filter() keeps the detections at 80 or above, and the tibble() compares the counts.

fire_hi <- fire_sf %>% filter(confidence >= 80)

tibble(
  threshold = c("all", "confidence >= 80"),
  detections = c(nrow(fire_sf), nrow(fire_hi))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  threshold        detections
  <chr>                 <int>
1 all                     897
2 confidence >= 80        164


The subset goes through the same as.ppp() and spattemp.density() steps with the bootstrap bandwidths, so only the data change.

fire_hi_owin <- fire_hi %>% select(DayofYear) %>% as.ppp() %>% .[kbb_owin]
kde_hi <- spattemp.density(fire_hi_owin, h = 45000, lambda = 17)

I plot three of the six days, with every detection on the top row and the high confidence subset below. zlim_conf is the range over both surfaces, so all six panels share one colour scale in the same unit as before.

The PlotThe Code














zlim_conf <- range(c(sapply(kde_yday_boot$z, range), sapply(kde_hi$z, range)))
par(mfcol = c(2, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0), cex.main = 1.8)
for (d in days[c(2, 4, 6)]) {
  plot_slice(kde_yday_boot, d, zlim = zlim_conf,
             main = paste("All, day", d))
  plot_slice(kde_hi, d, zlim = zlim_conf,
             main = paste("Conf >= 80, day", d))
}
mtext("All fires against confidence 80 and above, one scale", outer = TRUE, cex = 2.1, font = 2)
par(mfcol = c(1, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0))










TipAlternative explored



Eighty is FIRMS’s own cut-off for high confidence, and it is strict. Half the detections are below 67 and only 164 of 897 reach 80. So the bottom row uses under a fifth of the data.
Even with four fifths of the points gone, the hotspots are in the same places and move the same way through the season. Both surfaces are densities that integrate to one over space and time, so the smaller subset does not just come out dimmer. The thing to look for is the bright patches moving, and they do not.
This is a useful sanity check. A very different pattern in the high confidence subset would have meant the full-data maps were driven by noise. The pattern held, so they are not. The chapter skips the choice of threshold, which is a data quality decision. For the take-home I have to state and justify it.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
section: 9.3 Is It Space, Time, or Both
text:
9.3 Is It Space, Time, or Both
The K surface above tests for space-time interaction. It does not show whether there would be spatial clustering anyway with time ignored, which Exercise 2’s tools can check. unmark() drops the day marks. envelope() of spatstat simulates 39 random patterns in the same window around Lest, with global = TRUE for a simultaneous envelope.

fire_sp <- unmark(fire_yday_owin)
set.seed(1234)
L_sp <- envelope(fire_sp, Lest, nsim = 39, rank = 1,
                 global = TRUE, correction = "Ripley", verbose = FALSE)

The plot shows L(d) minus d against distance in metres. The solid line is the observed pattern and the dashed line at zero is complete spatial randomness. The grey band is the global envelope.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1)
plot(L_sp, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d (m)", ylab = "L(d) - r",
     main = "Spatial L function, time ignored, global envelope")










TipAlternative explored



The two results need to be read together. The L function shows the fires cluster in space when the whole year is put on one map. The STIK surface shows whether there is additional clustering once time is included.
If both show clustering, fires are drawn to the same places and also happen in bursts. If only the spatial one does, the bursts are just the dry season, and nearby fires are not setting each other off.
Here both show clustering. But the K surface used a constant intensity, so the dry season is still inside it. So I can only say fires cluster in space and in time. Whether the two interact is untested until I pass in lambda.
The chapter runs the second test without the first, so it cannot make that distinction. I need both to interpret the space-time result.

6.1 Determine the cut-off distance
The radius has to be big enough that every county has a neighbour. The book finds the distance from each county to its nearest neighbour and takes the largest. knearneigh() of spdep finds each county’s nearest centroid, knn2nb() turns that into a neighbour list, and nbdists() returns the great circle distances in km because of longlat = TRUE.

k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.57   38.01   39.07   44.52   61.79 


The largest nearest-neighbour distance is just under 62 km, so a 62 km radius gives every county at least one neighbour. which.max() shows which county has that longest distance.

[1] 85

hunan$County[which.max(k1dists)]

[1] "Taoyuan"








ImportantCheck that caught something



One county sets the cut-off for all 88, so I checked which one. It is Taoyuan, the same county that had the most neighbours under Queen. It is one of the largest counties on the map, fourth by area after Yuanling, Liuyang and Anhua. It also has a long irregular shape. So it touches many others, but its centroid is far from all of theirs. Under contiguity it is the best connected county in Hunan. Under distance it is the most isolated. 6.3 Plotting distance based neighbours
This is the same outline and nb plot as before, now for the 62 km list and the six nearest list.

The PlotThe Code














op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0), cex.main = 1.3)

The right choice depends on what the weights are for. For physical spillover, distance matters and the fixed radius reflects it. For comparing each county with its peers, the adaptive rule keeps the comparison fair.

9.2 Spatial lag as a sum of neighbouring values
If every neighbour gets a weight of one with style = "B", the same lag.listw() call gives the sum of the neighbours’ GDPPC. I join it back the same way.

b_weights <- lapply(wm_q, function(x) 0 * x + 1)
b_weights2 <- nb2listw(wm_q, glist = b_weights, style = "B")
lag_sum <- list(hunan$NAME_3, lag.listw(b_weights2, hunan$GDPPC))
lag.res <- as.data.frame(lag_sum)
colnames(lag.res) <- c("NAME_3", "lag_sum GDPPC")
hunan <- left_join(hunan, lag.res)







NoteLearning diary



0 * x + 1 is a small trick. Multiplying the neighbour list by zero and adding one gives a vector of ones, the same length as each county’s neighbour list. With style = "B" the ones are used as they are, so the lag is a plain sum.

text:
9.5 Visualising the spatial lags
A small helper function builds one quantile map per variable. tmap_arrange() puts GDPPC and three of the lags in a 2x2 grid. Each panel has its own quantile breaks, so the colours show ranks within a map, not RMB across maps.

The PlotThe Code














lag_map <- function(var, title, legend_title) {
  tm_shape(hunan) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.oranges"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legend_title,
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey60") +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(lag_map("GDPPC", "GDPPC",
                     "GDP per capita (RMB)"),
             lag_map("lag GDPPC", "Lag, neighbour average",
                     "Neighbour average (RMB)"),
             lag_map("lag_window_avg GDPPC", "Window average",
                     "Window average (RMB)"),
             lag_map("lag_sum GDPPC", "Lag sum",
                     "Sum of neighbours (RMB)"),
             ncol = 2)










NoteLearning diary



The two averages smooth the map. The north east block around Changsha gets stronger on both and spreads over most of the counties around the capital. The south east block around Chenzhou stays on the window average. On the neighbour average, though, the darkest class moves out to the ring of counties around it. This is because each county’s own value is left out, and Zixing’s neighbours are poorer than Zixing. Jishou and Zhongfang in the west and Lengshuijiang in the middle are single high spots, and they fade because their neighbours are poor.
The sum behaves differently. Taoyuan, the big county in the north with eleven neighbours, is in the middle class on the GDPPC map and the neighbour average. But it is in the darkest class on the sum. The sum rewards having many neighbours, however rich they are, so a lag sum map is partly a map of neighbour counts. It reflects the shape of the weights matrix as much as the values.

It is the sparsest, with 324 links against Queen’s 448, and no county gets more than six. The reason is scale. Hunan’s counties are mostly 40 to 60 km across. So a 62 km circle around a centroid rarely reaches past the first ring, and for the big counties in the west it does not even reach that.
The map shows where each rule gives many neighbours. Queen gives the most to the largest counties, because a big polygon touches many small ones. The 62 km rule gives the most to the middle band of small counties, where centroids are close together. It leaves the north west and the far south with one or two. The two rules give opposite answers about which counties are well connected.
This matters for the next chapter. The rule I pick decides which counties carry weight in every later statistic. Queen leans on the big western counties, and fixed distance leans on the small central ones.

Hunan is at about 112 east and 28 north, inside UTM zone 49 north, which is EPSG 32649. I expected the two methods to agree within a few hundred metres, but they do not. Projecting first moves the cut-off from 61.8 km to 58.3 km. A different county also sets it, Yuanling instead of Taoyuan.
The distance formula is not the cause. Great circle and planar UTM distances agree to well under a kilometre over 60 km. The cause is the centroids. st_centroid() on lon/lat treats degrees as if they were flat. For a big irregular county this puts the centroid a few kilometres from where it should be. Taoyuan is big and irregular, so its centroid moved the most, and its nearest neighbour got closer.
The book’s 62 km radius still works, because 62 is above both numbers. But the hidden warning affects more than small errors. It changed which county is the most isolated. I will project first from now on.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
10.3 A preview of Moran’s I
The next chapter asks whether GDPPC is spatially autocorrelated. The lag I just computed already gives half of the answer. If a county’s value predicts its neighbours’ average, the points on this plot line up. lm() fits the line so its slope can go in the subtitle. geom_text_repel() of ggrepel labels the richest counties and the ones with the richest neighbours, without covering the points or the line.

The PlotThe Code














lag_df <- hunan %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(NAME_3, GDPPC, lag = `lag GDPPC`)

fit <- lm(lag ~ GDPPC, data = lag_df)

ggplot(lag_df, aes(GDPPC, lag)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(lag_df$lag), colour = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(lag_df$GDPPC), colour = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text_repel(data = lag_df %>% filter(GDPPC > 60000 | lag > 45000),
                  aes(label = NAME_3), size = 3.5, seed = 42,
                  box.padding = 0.5, min.segment.length = 0) +
  labs(x = "GDPPC (RMB)", y = "Neighbour average GDPPC (RMB)",
       title = "Each county against the average of its Queen neighbours",
       subtitle = paste0("Slope of the fitted line, ",
                         round(coef(fit)[2], 3))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13))










TipAlternative explored



The slope of that line is Moran’s I, 0.30 here. I first thought both variables had to be standardised for this to hold, but they do not. With row-standardised weights each row sums to one. So the neighbour average of a centred variable is the neighbour average minus the overall mean. The least squares slope of the lag on GDPPC then equals the Moran’s I formula exactly, and rescaling both axes would not change it. It is positive, so rich counties tend to have rich neighbours. moran.test() in the next chapter should return the same 0.30 with a p-value.
The labelled points are the ones off the line. Changsha, Wangcheng, Liuyang and Ningxiang are top right, rich with rich neighbours. This is the capital and its ring. Zixing and Lengshuijiang are bottom right, rich counties with poor neighbours. Both are mining and industrial towns, so the wealth stays local and does not spill over. Pingjiang is the reverse. It is a poor county whose neighbours average over 55,000 because it borders the Changsha ring.
The local statistics in the next chapter pick out these off-line counties one by one. That chapter will also test whether 0.30 is more than chance.

text:
10.1 Choa Chu Kang planning area
Gest() of spatstat computes G with the border correction. The black line is the estimate and the orange dashed line is G under CSR.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
G_CK <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")
plot(G_CK, xlim = c(0, 500), xlab = "d (m)",
     col = c("black", "#D55E00"),
     main = "G function, Choa Chu Kang")





H0: childcare centres in Choa Chu Kang are randomly distributed.
H1: they are not.







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book says to reject if p is below 0.001. But an envelope never prints a p-value, and 999 simulations cannot reach 0.001 anyway. By the rule in the Clark-Evans diary, a pointwise envelope from 999 simulations at the default rank of 1 is a two-sided test at alpha = 2/1000 = 0.002 at each distance.
So I reject at a distance if the black curve leaves the grey band there, at 0.002 rather than 0.001.


envelope() of spatstat simulates 999 CSR patterns in the same window and computes G for each. Black is the observed G, orange dashed is G under CSR and grey is the range of the simulations.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
G_CK.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, nsim = 999, verbose = FALSE)
plot(G_CK.csr, xlab = "d (m)", col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "G against 999 simulations of CSR, Choa Chu Kang")




The black curve leaves the band only at the shortest distances. It jumps to about 0.19 within the first metre or two. So roughly a fifth of the centres have another centre almost on top of them, most likely two operators in the same block. The band catches up at about 45 m, and after that the curve stays inside it.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The grey band looks like a confidence interval and is often read as one, but it is not.
Floch et al. say this directly. “The envelope should not be interpreted as a confidence interval around the indicator being studied: it indicates the critical values of the test.” The band is the range the simulated patterns covered, not a range of plausible values for my curve.
So my plot titles name the simulations instead of calling it a confidence band, and I read every grey band on this page as critical values.

     main = "F against 999 simulations of CSR, Choa Chu Kang")




Observed F runs below the CSR line, which is the direction clustering predicts. But it stays inside the grey band at every distance, so F by itself finds no departure from CSR.

G and F point opposite ways for the same pattern, which confused me until I drew it out.
Clustered points have close neighbours, so G climbs fast. But clustering also leaves big empty gaps, so a random location is far from any point and F climbs slowly. So clustering puts G above the line and F below it. Once I understood that, the plots stopped looking contradictory.

envelope() with Kest, 99 simulations and global = TRUE builds one simultaneous band for all distances. Black is the observed K, orange dashed at zero is CSR and grey is the global envelope. The legend is off so it cannot cover the band.

The PlotThe Code

                     global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

     ylab = "K(d) - pi d^2 (km sq)", legend = FALSE,
     col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "K against CSR, global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")




The observed curve rises above zero, to about 0.3 km sq by 800 m. But the global band is about 0.58 km sq wide on each side at every distance, so the curve never comes close to leaving it. Tested at all distances together, K does not reject CSR for Choa Chu Kang.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book writes glocal = TRUE here and for L, a typo for global = TRUE. envelope() has no glocal argument, so R passes it through ... to Kest(), which silently ignores it. So the book’s K and L envelopes are pointwise, even though the code seems to ask for global ones. I copied it at first without noticing, which shows it is easy to miss. I use global = TRUE.
Global matters because the test is repeated at dozens of r values, and reporting the ones that cross pushes the false positive rate well above the stated alpha. A global envelope corrects for that and a pointwise one does not. With rank = 1 and 99 simulations, the global band is a single test at alpha = 1/100 across all distances at once.
A global band contains the pointwise band from the same simulations, so it is harder for the curve to leave. The G and F results above use pointwise bands, so they are weaker evidence than the K and L results here. The book never says so. I redo G with a global band in Beyond the Exercise.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: 14.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
text:
14.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
Everything so far compares childcare centres to a pattern where any point in Singapore is equally likely, including reservoirs, the airport, industrial estates and military land. At least Jurong Island was dropped with the offshore subzones at the start.
Floch et al. raise this for French pharmacies, where regulation ties locations to population. They say CSR “does not appear to be the most relevant” reference there. Childcare centres similarly follow housing. So the clustering result may only tell me that Singapore’s residents are clustered, which I already knew.
The reading suggests a fix. Kinhom() drops the assumption of constant intensity and compares the pattern against a null that uses the observed intensity. If the centres still clump beyond that, the clustering is real. If not, it was caused by population.
density() with bw.diggle estimates the intensity surface for Choa Chu Kang, and range() checks its values.

lambda_ck <- density(childcare_ck_ppp, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
range(lambda_ck$v, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 5.030384e-10 4.086766e-05








NoteLearning diary



My surface is entirely positive, but I clamp it anyway.
The book’s own output in section 4.7.1 has a density range starting at -6.58e-21. That is floating point noise from the edge correction, not a real negative density, and it does not show on the plot.
It only matters when the surface goes to rpoispp() for the simulation below, which refuses a negative intensity with a “negative probability” error that does not say where the negative came from. Whether you hit it depends on your data.
Adding one line now is easier than debugging that later.


The clamp sets any negative cell to zero, then counts how many there were.

lambda_pos <- lambda_ck
lambda_pos$v[lambda_pos$v < 0] <- 0

# confirm whether the clamp actually had anything to do
sum(lambda_ck$v < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0


Kinhom() of spatstat computes the inhomogeneous K with that surface as lambda, plotted against pi d^2 the same way as K above.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
Kinhom_ck <- Kinhom(childcare_ck_ppp, lambda = lambda_pos,
                    correction = "Ripley")
plot(Kinhom_ck, (. - pi * r^2) / 1e6 ~ r,
     ylab = "Kinhom(d) - pi d^2 (km sq)", xlab = "d (m)",
     col = c("black", "#D55E00"),
     main = "Inhomogeneous K, intensity taken from the data")




With the intensity taken from the data, the curve falls below zero and keeps falling, to about -0.7 km sq by 800 m. Taken literally, this means the centres have fewer neighbours than the local intensity predicts.
envelope() with Kinhom and simulate = expression(rpoispp(lambda_pos)) draws 39 patterns from the estimated intensity instead of from CSR. Black is observed, orange dashed is the mean of the simulated patterns and grey is their pointwise range. The legend is off so it cannot cover the band.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
Kinhom_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kinhom,
                          simulate = expression(rpoispp(lambda_pos)),
                          nsim = 39, verbose = FALSE)
plot(Kinhom_ck.csr, (. - pi * r^2) / 1e6 ~ r, xlab = "d (m)",
     ylab = "Kinhom(d) - pi d^2 (km sq)", legend = FALSE,
     col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "Inhomogeneous K against a population-shaped null")




Here the observed curve stays close to zero and inside the band at every distance. Once the local intensity is accounted for, Choa Chu Kang shows no extra clustering.






ImportantCheck that caught something



The black curve here ends near -0.05 km sq, but the previous plot of the same data ended near -0.7. They are different estimates. In the earlier plot I passed lambda_pos, built from these same points with a narrow bw.diggle bandwidth. So each centre’s intensity includes its own kernel and comes out too high, which pulls K down. Inside envelope() I did not pass lambda, so Kinhom() estimated it itself and left each point out of its own intensity. That leave-one-out estimate is the one to trust, so the deep dip earlier is mostly an artefact.








TipAlternative explored



This uses the same K function for a different question. Kest asks whether centres are more clustered than a uniform scatter. Kinhom asks whether they are more clustered than the local intensity already implies.
Compare this plot with the Kest one further up. Any gap left here is clustering that population density does not explain.
One caveat is that the null comes from the same data it is tested against, so it is not independent evidence. Floch et al. warn that bias appears when the smoothing window is close in size to the r values being tested.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
14.2 Cumulative Against Density
K counts every neighbour out to r, so it is cumulative. A bump at 400 metres could come from tight clustering at 50 metres still carried in the total.
The pair correlation function counts in a ring at distance r instead of a disc out to r. So it shows the distance where clustering happens, not where it has built up.
pcf() of spatstat estimates it. It shoots up near zero distance, so I cap the y axis at 4 to keep the rest readable.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
pcf_ck <- pcf(childcare_ck_ppp)
plot(pcf_ck, main = "Pair correlation, Choa Chu Kang",
     xlab = "d (m)", ylim = c(0, 4), legendpos = "topright",
     col = c("black", "#0072B2", "#D55E00"))
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")










TipAlternative explored



Under randomness the pair correlation is 1, shown by the dashed line. Above 1 means more neighbours at that exact distance than chance would give.
Its advantage over K is that it pins down the distance of the clustering. Its disadvantage is that only a cumulative function can detect clusters of clusters. They answer different questions, so one does not replace the other.

section: 14.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
text:
14.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
The earlier G test used a pointwise envelope, which inflates the false positive rate across the r values tested. Here I rerun it with envelope() set to global = TRUE and rank = 1 over 39 simulations.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
G_ck.global <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, nsim = 39, rank = 1,
                        global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(G_ck.global, xlab = "d (m)", ylim = c(0, 1),
     col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "G with a global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")




The curve stays inside the global band at every distance, including the short-distance jump that left the pointwise band. The band’s upper edge at zero distance is already about 0.27, above the 0.19 jump.






TipAlternative explored



The correction makes a global band wider than a pointwise one, so it is harder to reject the null, as intended.
If the curve still leaves the band, the result survives the multiple testing problem. If not, the original finding was partly an artefact of testing at every r and reporting the crossings.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
14.4 A Second Opinion on Randomness
All the tests so far are distance based. A quadrat test, from the other family, divides the region into cells and compares the counts against a Poisson expectation. quadrat.test() of spatstat runs it on a 4 by 4 grid.

quadrat_ck <- quadrat.test(childcare_ck_ppp, nx = 4, ny = 4)
quadrat_ck


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
X2 = 21.603, df = 12, p-value = 0.08444
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 13 tiles (irregular windows)








WarningIssue I hit



I first stored this as qt, which is base R’s t-distribution quantile function. R refused with “cannot change value of locked binding”.
It is the same mistake as naming something c or df, so I should check a name is free first.








ImportantCheck that caught something



The quadrat test does not agree with Clark-Evans.
Clark-Evans gave R of 0.84 with p of 0.0089, rejecting randomness for Choa Chu Kang. The quadrat test on the same points gives p of 0.084, so it does not. On one dataset, the two tests reach opposite conclusions at the five percent level.
Neither is wrong, because they measure different things. Clark-Evans looks at nearest neighbour distances, so it notices points in tight pairs. The quadrat test only counts points per cell, so a pattern can be clumpy inside cells and still even across them.
The tile count also changed. I asked for a four by four grid, which is sixteen cells, but the output says thirteen tiles and twelve degrees of freedom. Three cells fell outside the planning area boundary and were dropped, and twelve is thirteen minus one. So the tested grid is not the one I specified.








TipAlternative explored



The quadrat result depends entirely on the grid I picked. A different nx and ny would change it.
This is the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem again, which I met in Exercise 1 when aggregating subzones to planning areas. The reading gives it as one of the main reasons to prefer distance-based methods.

CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book reads a shapefile that really is in SVY21 but has the wrong EPSG code attached. The coordinates are fine and only the label is wrong, so the book fixes the label with st_set_crs(3414).
My file has a different problem. It really is WGS84. The bounding box runs 103.6 to 104.1 across and 1.16 to 1.47 up, and those are degrees. In SVY21 the values would be metres in the tens of thousands.

What helped was reading the bounding box instead of skipping past it. Degrees look like 103.8 and metres look like 28,000.
What I learned is that st_set_crs fixes a wrong label, while st_transform changes the actual coordinates. I should check which one is broken before picking.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
7.1 Land Acquisition Analysis
In this scenario the authority wants to widen the existing cycling paths and needs 5 metres of reserved land on either side. The task is to work out how much land that is.
dist = 5 in st_buffer() uses the units of the layer’s coordinate system. In a projected system like SVY21 that is metres. In degrees it is less clear. With the s2 engine on, which is the sf default, a buffer on geographic coordinates is computed on the sphere and dist is taken as metres. With s2 off, the same call reads 5 as five degrees. That is a buffer of some 550 km on every side, and it still runs without error. Working in SVY21 means the answer does not depend on that setting.
The cycling path already came in SVY21, so this transform changes nothing. I kept it so the code does not rely on LTA always shipping it that way. It costs nothing and makes the assumption clear.

Confirming the projectionBuffering the pathsComputing the areaAdding up the total


st_transform() to 3414, then st_crs() to confirm.

cyclingpath3414 <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
st_crs(cyclingpath3414)$epsg

[1] 3414




st_buffer() builds the 5 metre buffers. nQuadSegs = 30 keeps the rounded ends smooth.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath3414, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)



st_area() inside mutate() gives the area of each buffer.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))



sum() adds the buffer areas together.

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]





To see what this looks like on the ground, I clip the buffers to one subzone, Tampines West. filter() picks the subzone and st_intersection() cuts the buffers to its boundary.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz3414 %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

plot() draws Tampines West and lays the clipped buffers over it in orange.

The PlotThe Code

     col = "#F7F4EC", border = "grey55", lwd = 0.8,
     main = "Five metre reserve along cycling paths, Tampines West")

     col = "#D55E00", border = NA)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
8.2 Data Wrangling
The goal is one row per subzone with six fields. YOUNG is ages 0 to 24, ECONOMY ACTIVE is 25 to 64, and AGED is 65 and over. DEPENDENCY divides the young plus the aged by the economically active.

Aggregating and pivotingSelecting the age bands by nameDeriving the dependency ratioChecking the totals


group_by() and summarise() add up the residents in each subzone and age group, then pivot_wider() of tidyr spreads the age groups into columns.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP)

The book skips the next step, but it turned out to matter a lot. names() shows the order of the age columns.

names(popdata2024)

 [1] "PA"          "SZ"          "0_to_4"      "10_to_14"    "15_to_19"   
 [6] "20_to_24"    "25_to_29"    "30_to_34"    "35_to_39"    "40_to_44"   
[11] "45_to_49"    "50_to_54"    "55_to_59"    "5_to_9"      "60_to_64"   
[16] "65_to_69"    "70_to_74"    "75_to_79"    "80_to_84"    "85_to_89"   
[21] "90_and_over"


The book builds the three age bands by column number. But in the list above, the age groups are not in age order.
This comes from the summarise step. summarise() sorts its rows by the grouping columns. AG is text, so the age groups are sorted as text. pivot_wider() then creates the columns in that sorted order. As text, 5_to_9 comes after 55_to_59, so it sits at position 14 instead of 12.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book uses rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[12]) for YOUNG and similar column ranges for the other bands. With my columns, those numbers make YOUNG pick up the 50 to 54 band instead of 5 to 9. ECONOMY ACTIVE ends up counting primary school children. I select the bands by name instead.








WarningIssue I hit



Like the projection problem, this does not throw an error. It just gives a wrong dependency ratio, and every map after it looks normal.
I nearly skipped names(popdata2024). That one line caught the problem.




Selecting by name removes the dependency on column order. Three character vectors hold the band names.

young_ag <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19", "20_to_24")

active_ag <- c("25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44",
               "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64")

aged_ag <- c("65_to_69", "70_to_74", "75_to_79",
             "80_to_84", "85_to_89", "90_and_over")

I also add a guard against this problem. stopifnot() stops the render if a future release renames or drops a band, instead of letting a wrong number through.

stopifnot(all(c(young_ag, active_ag, aged_ag) %in% names(popdata2024)))



rowSums() over across(all_of(...)) adds up each band by name, then select() keeps the six fields plus the keys.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(
    YOUNG = rowSums(across(all_of(young_ag))),
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(across(all_of(active_ag))),
    AGED = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_ag))),
    TOTAL = rowSums(across(all_of(c(young_ag, active_ag, aged_ag)))),
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



Next I check the result. The three bands should add up to the total, and the ratio for Singapore overall should be near 0.7. summarise() computes both.

popdata2024 %>%
  summarise(
    young = sum(YOUNG),
    active = sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`),
    aged = sum(AGED),
    total = sum(TOTAL),
    bands_match_total = sum(YOUNG) + sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) + sum(AGED) == sum(TOTAL),
    overall_dependency = (sum(YOUNG) + sum(AGED)) / sum(`ECONOMY ACTIVE`)
  )

ImportantCheck that caught something



The bands add to 4,189,460, which fits Singapore’s resident population of a little over 4 million, and they match the total exactly. The overall ratio is 0.732, which is in the expected range.
Both had to be right before I trusted any map on this page. If I had used the book’s column numbers, the problem would have shown up in this check.

  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

                            position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_title("qtm() with its default bins", size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")




qtm() is quick, but the default bins are a problem. The legend runs 0 to 10 in steps of two. Almost every subzone is under 1, so the island lands in the palest class with one dark polygon near Changi. The map is not wrong, but it shows very little.






NoteLearning diary



One subzone with a ratio of 10 is enough to spoil the default bins for the other 237 subzones that have a ratio. The custom breaks section below deals with this.
It is also why I stop using qtm() here. To change the bins, the palette or the legend I have to pass tm_polygons() arguments through it anyway, as I did with the legend above. So from here on I write tm_shape() and tm_polygons() in full.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1

10.2 Equal Interval Classification
style = "equal" cuts the range of values into five classes of the same width instead.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal interval, equal widths per class", size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")




The two maps use the same column but look very different.
Quantile puts the same number of subzones in each class, so the breaks come out at 0.64, 0.70, 0.74 and 0.82. These all fall where most of the data is, and the map clearly separates the central and eastern subzones.
Equal interval cuts 0 to 10 into five equal parts. Nearly everything falls in the first one, so the island goes pale with a single dark polygon. From that map alone I would think dependency hardly varies in Singapore, which is not true.
Both maps show the same numbers correctly. But one subzone at 10 makes the equal interval version almost useless. I only saw this by putting the two side by side.

section: 10.3 Plotting a Choropleth Map with Custom Breaks
text:
10.3 Plotting a Choropleth Map with Custom Breaks
I look at the numbers before choosing break points. summary() gives the quartiles and the extremes.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 


The middle half of the subzones sits between 0.675 and 0.814, so breaks at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90 separate most of the data. But the maximum is 10, so I also need a top class above 1.00 for those subzones. breaks in tm_scale_intervals() takes n+1 values, including a minimum and maximum, so six classes need seven values.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00, 10)),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Custom breaks read from the summary", size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book’s breaks are c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00) and stop at 1.00, but the summary shows a maximum of 10. Subzones above 1.00 fall outside the classes, but in my first render tmap still painted them in the darkest class. So the legend said the top class ended at 1.00 while it held a subzone at 10. I added a seventh break at 10 so the top class, 1.00 to 10, shows what it holds.

text:
11.1 Using ColorBrewer Palettes
values in tm_scale_intervals() picks the palette. This map reuses the quantile classes from above and only swaps the default blues for the ColorBrewer oranges.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.oranges"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("The quantile classes in brewer.oranges", size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")




A minus prefix reverses the ramp. Dark now means a low ratio, which feels backwards. It is only useful when the low values are the focus.

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "-brewer.oranges"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("The same ramp reversed, dark now means low", size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book shows palettes with "brewer.greens" and "-brewer.greens", and uses the reversed greens again for the map style. I avoid green as a data colour because red and green are the pair most colour-blind readers struggle with. I use the blues default and "brewer.oranges" for the same two ideas, and "brewer.or_rd" for the style map.

Giving fill two column names makes tmap draw one map per variable. fill.free = FALSE puts both on one shared equal interval scale, so the same shade means the same number of residents in both panels. tm_facets_vstack() stacks the two maps one above the other, so each one gets the full width of the page.

  tm_polygons(fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
              fill.free = FALSE,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residents (count)",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues")) +
